title: DeepSeek Harness Desktop plugin catalog
description: Editor-time mirror of `parseCatalog` in the desktop app's packages/market/lib/fetch.js. It exists so a submitter sees a mistake while typing; it is NOT the gate. The installer never reads this file, and JSON Schema cannot express the two rules that matter most — that the digest matches the bytes, and that the tarball's manifest agrees with the row — so `validate.yml` drives the app's own module instead of this document. When the two disagree, fetch.js wins and this file is the bug.

$schema.description: Editor hint. Ignored by the installer, which reads only `version` and `plugins`.

version.description: Catalog format version. `parseCatalog` throws ERR_MARKET_CATALOG on anything but the literal 1 — the envelope fails loud rather than being guessed at, because a version we do not know means we are not reading what we think we are reading.

plugins.description: The offered rows, in the order the app lists them. A malformed row is dropped and reported rather than failing the catalog, so one bad submission cannot hide every good one — which is exactly why CI asserts `dropped` is empty instead of only asserting the fetch succeeded.

id.description: Catalog identity. The installer never reads it (it looks a listing up by `name`), so this repo requires `id` to equal `name` -- two identities for one plugin is two identities that eventually disagree. The pattern is SAFE_ID from fetch.js verbatim: an id may become a directory name in the installer, so both segments must start alphanumeric and a bare `..` is unrepresentable. A repeated id is dropped as `duplicate-id` (first row wins), because a later row shadowing an earlier one is a cheap way to substitute a plugin. SAFE_ID permits uppercase and the installer's own isPluginName does not, which is why `name` carries the tighter pattern below and `id` must equal it.

name.description: The npm PACKAGE NAME -- not a label, despite fetch.js's JSDoc calling it a display name. The installer finds the listing by matching this field, then refuses the download unless the tarball's own package.json name equals it ("the package is X, not Y as the catalog said"), and writes the package to profiles/desktop/node_modules/<name>. It is also what the Plugins tab shows as the row label, so a plugin cannot currently carry a separate human-readable title. The pattern is PACKAGE_NAME from the app's registry.js: lowercase only, one optional scope segment, both segments starting alphanumeric -- stricter than npm's own rule, because a name that reaches Node resolution with `..` in it is a traversal primitive.

title.description: Human-readable label shown in the Marketplace tab. OPTIONAL: parseCatalog falls back to  when it is absent, so an older catalog stays valid. Supply it --  is the npm package name and a resolution key, and making it double as a label is why this field was added.

version.description: One concrete semver release -- 1.4.2, 0.1.0-rc.8, build metadata and all -- and it must equal the version in the tarball's package.json. fetch.js does not parse it at all (any non-empty string passes), so a range or a file: spec reaches the installer and is refused there with a 422; this pattern and the isPluginVersion call in CI are what catch it earlier. Not a range, because the value is written into the profile manifest and read by the next pnpm install in that directory.

publisher.description: Who publishes it, shown next to the name. Not verified against anything — it is a label, not an attestation.

description.description: One sentence, shown under the name in the Plugins tab. The list gives it one row.

tarball.description: A GitHub Release asset of THIS repo. fetch.js requires only https with no credentials — the tarball host is deliberately not allowlisted, because what binds these bytes to this catalog is the digest, not the host, and Release assets redirect to a CDN host nobody would want to keep a list of. The tighter pattern here is this repo's own policy, not the app's: plugins are never published to npm, so a row pointing anywhere else is a mistake worth catching in the editor.

integrity.description: SRI digest of the exact release-asset bytes, `sha512-<base64>` (sha256 is accepted by fetch.js but sha512 is what `npm pack` and the release workflow emit). Exactly one hash: SRI allows a whitespace-separated list, which immediately raises the question of how many have to match, so the format admits one. A missing or unparsable digest is a refusal, never a skipped check — the digest is the only thing standing between the app and arbitrary code.

$comment.description: Maintainer note. Ignored by the installer and by the gate, except that `validate.yml` reads nothing from it — do not encode policy here.
